First, we multiply the two functions, as follows: \begin{align*} \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} \left(p(x) \cdot q(x)\right) &=\lim_\limits{x \to \infty} \left(2x \cdot 7x^4 \right)\\[5pt] &=\lim_\limits{x \to \infty}\left(\left(2 \cdot 7 \right) x^{1+4} \right) \\[5pt] &=\lim_\limits{x \to \infty}\left(14 \cdot x^{5} \right) \\[5pt] & = 14 \cdot \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} x^{5} \end{align*}

The graph $y = x^{5}$ is power function with an odd positive power and therefore has the property that \[ \lim_{x \to \infty } x^{5} = \infty. \]

Multiplication by the positive constant $14$ does not affect the limit at infinity. So, we have \begin{align*} 14 \cdot \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} x^{5} = \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} x^{5} = \infty. \end{align*}

Therefore, we conclude that \[ \lim_\limits{x \rightarrow \infty}\left( 14x^{5}\right) = \infty. \]

example.title: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a Power Function With an Odd Power

question.explanation:
First, let's calculate $x^5 \cdot q(x)\mathbin{:}$ \[ x^5 \cdot q(x) = x^5 \cdot (4x) = 4x^6. \]

When we divide the two functions $p(x)$ and $x^5 \cdot q(x),$ we get a constant, and the limit of a constant is just the constant itself:

\begin{align*} \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{p(x)}{x^5 \cdot q(x)} & = \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{3x^6}{4x^6}\\[5pt] &= \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{3}{4} \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{3}{4}} \end{align*}

question.explanation:
First, let's calculate $x^2\cdot r(x):$ \[ x^2 \cdot r(x) = x^2 \cdot \left( -2x^8 \right) = -2x^{10} \]

When we multiply the two functions $x^{2}\cdot r(x)$ and $s(x)$, we get a constant, and the limit of a constant is just the constant itself:

\begin{align*} \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} \left(x^2\cdot r(x)\cdot s(x)\right) &=\lim_\limits{x \to \infty}\left( -2x^{10} \cdot \dfrac{11}{x^{10}}\right) \\[5pt] &= \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} -22 \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-22} \end{align*}
